# Introduction

`ndopred` applies the **IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria v3.1** (IUCN 2012)
using the interpretation given in the **Guidelines for Using the IUCN Red List
Categories and Criteria v16** (IUCN Standards and Petitions Committee, March
2024), for a **national (Czech) Red List** built from NDOP occurrence records.
The **Guidelines for Application of IUCN Red List Criteria at Regional and
National Levels v4.0** (IUCN 2012, "RG") give the regional step. Section numbers
refer to the Guidelines v16 unless stated otherwise. `methodology/gap_analysis.md`
records the audit of the package against these documents, the decisions AOPK
took, and what each phase changed.

## Four states of a value

The method rests on keeping apart four things that are easily confused:

| State | What it is | Who sets it | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Calculated** | measured from the records: EOO, AOO, counts, raw changes | ndopred | the NDOP snapshot and the run configuration |
| **Evidenced** | a condition, number or threat documented by an assessor, with author, date, justification and source | the assessor | the evidence file |
| **Proposed** | the category the criteria give from what is calculated and evidenced, with its plausible range and what is still missing | the rule engine | the export and the species card |
| **Approved** | the final category, checked against the evidence and approved by the group experts | the group experts | the evidence file (final category and approval rows) |

A calculated value is not evidence: a cluster count is not a number of
locations, and a change in recorded AOO is not a reduction. A proposal is not a
category: only an approved final category is one. Each part of this vignette
follows one step: from records to calculated values (part I), from those and
the evidence to a proposal (part II), from the proposal to an approved
category (part III), and how the method is checked (part IV).

Where the IUCN rules and ease of use pull apart, ndopred follows the rules and
says so: an unknown condition stays unknown instead of being guessed, a
restricted taxon is a D2 *candidate* until a threat is described, and no
category is final without approval.

# Part I. From records to calculated values

## 1. Records: snapshots and flags

Each download is an **immutable snapshot** (`ndop_snapshot()`): the records and
their points, lines and polygons as NDOP returned them, with the query, the
download time and the versions. Stored as RDS (by default in
`Documents/ndop_snapshots`, outside the repository, since snapshots hold exact
coordinates and observer names), a snapshot lets any assessment be rerun on
exactly the same records; `latest_snapshot()` finds it again. NDOP data are
never edited.

`flag_records()` then adds one flag per test and the first exclusion reason.
**Nothing is deleted.** The rules, agreed with AOPK:

* `VEROH` (credibility after the guarantor's review): 0 not yet validated and 1
  credible are used; 6 and 9 (erroneous) are excluded; 3 (less credible) is
  always used, and flagged only when more than 10 % of the taxon's records
  carry it. A validation mark proposed while the guarantee is open
  (`VALIDACE`) is only flagged.
* Records of another taxon are excluded; names match exactly, because the NDOP
  query also returns hybrids and aggregates.
* Negative findings are kept as non-detections, out of the presence metrics.
* Records without coordinates (including hidden ones) or outside Czechia are
  excluded.
* Literature and collection records (recognised by markers in `ZDROJ`: a card
  index, collection, museum, herbarium, atlas, literature data or a journal
  volume with pages) and suspected duplicates are flagged only. The rndop
  export has no source-type field, so the literature flag is a heuristic.
* A record dated as a range (`DATUM_OD` to `DATUM_DO`) belongs to a time window
  only if the whole range lies inside it.

Records can also be excluded or re-included by an assessor, by `ID_NALEZ` and
with a reason, in the evidence file (section 12); the record keeps its row.

## 2. Spatial metrics

**AOO** is the count of occupied cells times the cell area (§4.10.2, eq. 4.1) on
the reference **2 × 2 km** grid (§4.10.3). Because AOO depends on where the grid
starts, `calculate_aoo()` keeps the **minimum** over grid origins, as §4.10.2
requires. It tests a 4 × 4 lattice of origins and, for up to 150 distinct
positions, also every origin at which the count can change (the positions of
the points modulo the cell size), which finds the exact minimum where a cell
matters most, near the CR and EN thresholds of B2. The criterion B2 value is
always this current-window minimum on 2 × 2 km; other grid sizes are for
display only.

Positional precision (`CXPRESNOST`, metres; 0 = exact) and NDOP's record
polygons and lines give AOO a range at the same origin (§3.2):

* the **minimum** puts each record whose precision disc or polygon reaches into
  other cells into a cell already occupied, whenever it can reach one;
* the **maximum** gives each such record a cell of its own, whenever it can.

The range bounds the *observed* AOO. Observed AOO is itself a plausible
*lower* bound on the true AOO of an under-recorded taxon (§4.10.8); an upper
bound from habitat maps is not implemented.

**EOO** is a minimum convex polygon (§4.9). Discontinuities and disjunctions are
deliberately *not* excluded. Its range comes from the same sources: the
minimum leaves out records less precise than 2 km and flagged less-credible
records; the maximum is the hull of every precision disc and polygon. Where a
hull cannot be built, `reconcile_eoo_aoo()` substitutes AOO, per the rule that
EOO is never smaller than AOO.

**Clusters.** `calculate_locations()` counts 5 km distance clusters. They are
reported as clusters, never as locations: a location is "a geographically or
ecologically distinct area in which a single threatening event can rapidly
affect all individuals of the taxon present" (§4.11), defined by a threat the
records do not show.

## 3. Time windows and generation length

The windows are an AOPK convention (D5): the current window is the 17 years up
to the reference year (**2010–2026** for 2026), and the trend compares it with
**2000–2016**, the same window ten years earlier. Ten years is the period of
criterion A unless three generations are longer; then the comparison window
moves back by three generations (`ndopred_config(window = 17)`, with
`trend_shift` derived from the generation length). The reference year is always
explicit; nothing reads the system clock.

**Generation length** comes from `generation_lengths()`, a table with one row
per NDOP taxonomic group (`KAT_TAX`), unless the assessor gives one for the
taxon. Every group is set to **1 year** for now, a placeholder AOPK will refine.
Up to 3.3 years a generation length changes nothing: criterion A uses 10 years
until three generations exceed it, and C1 uses 3, 5 and 10 years until one, two
and three generations exceed them. Each result row reports the value used and
its source.

* **Criterion B** describes the **current** distribution: §4.9 states that EOO
  and AOO "should not include areas where the species no longer exists". EOO,
  AOO and clusters use the current window.
* **The trend** compares the two windows on a **single shared grid origin**, so
  that the change is not an artefact of two different grids. The windows'
  midpoints are 10 years apart, the period of criterion A2. They share
  2010–2016, and records from those years count in both, which damps the
  measured change.

## 4. Trends and data tiers

`trend_estimate()` classifies each taxon's data into the tiers of the review
(Table 5) and computes the trend the tier allows:

* **T0**, records only: the raw change in AOO (one grid origin for both windows)
  and in EOO as an alpha-hull. §4.9 recommends the alpha-hull, not the convex
  hull, "for assessing reductions or continuing declines in EOO"; it is built
  on one point per occupied 2 × 2 km cell so that it follows the range rather
  than the density of recording. The comparison window is also moved two years
  earlier and later, and the range of changes is the interval (start-year
  sensitivity, review §7.4). A diagnostic, not a population trend.
* **T1**, an effort layer of the group (`ndop_effort()`: every record of the
  NDOP group, reduced to cells and anonymous visits; for large groups a random
  sample of cadastral units): relative occupancy on the cells recorded for the
  group in both windows, with a bootstrap interval. An explicitly labelled
  interim proxy.
* **T2**, repeat visits of the group around the taxon: a multi-season
  occupancy-detection model (`spOccupancy::tPGOcc()`), occupancy with a linear
  trend over years, detection with the visit's list length. A trend in
  occupancy, not in mature individuals (review §7.3), so basis (c). Run when
  `trend_settings(occupancy_model = TRUE)`; it takes minutes per taxon.
* **T3**, counts from standardized monitoring projects that AOPK lists
  (`monitoring_projects`): an abundance index, a log-linear model of counts on
  site and year, basis (b). The only source of an estimated decline (C1) and of
  a fluctuation diagnosis from records.

The best available tier gives the reduction *indication*, with its interval
as the plausible range. It becomes evidence only when an assessor confirms it.

# Part II. From calculated values and evidence to a proposal

## 5. One engine, three layers of input

All entry points (both Shiny apps, `assess_species()`, `batch_assess()` and the
deprecated `summarize_assessment()`) call the same engine:
`assessment_inputs()` → `assess_criteria()` → `categorise()`. No other code
holds thresholds or category logic, so bulk and single-taxon mode give the same
result for the same inputs.

| Layer | Examples | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Data** | EOO, AOO, record counts | calculated from the records |
| **Indication** | cluster count for locations; the trend estimate for reduction and decline; NDOP counts for mature individuals; localities for subpopulations | derived from the records |
| **Evidence** | severe fragmentation, the most serious plausible threat, threat-defined locations, continuing decline, population estimates, a confirmed reduction | the assessor |

Every condition is TRUE, FALSE or **UNKNOWN**. The proposal uses the evidence
where there is some, otherwise the indication. An unknown condition with no
indication does not count towards the proposal, but it is never read as FALSE:
it widens the plausible range and is listed as needing evidence. Numbers can be
ranges, `min`/`best`/`max`: the proposal uses the best estimate, and each end
of the plausible range uses the end that lowers or raises the risk (§3.2).

Guidelines Table 3.1 sets a minimum data quality per criterion: below it, the
criterion "is considered not to have been met". Evidence below the minimum of
its criterion (a suspected decline for B(b) or C2; inferred numbers for C, D or
C2a(i); an inferred decline for C1) is documented but not used.

## 6. The proposal

`categorise()` returns:

* the **proposed category**: the highest category met (§2.3), with every
  criterion met at that category;
* the **criteria** in ndopred's established format (`B1ab(ii); B2ab(ii)`) and
  in IUCN Annex 2 notation (`B1ab(ii)+2ab(ii)`);
* the **support**: `evidence` when nothing behind the proposal rests on an
  indication or an unknown, `indication` otherwise;
* what **needs evidence**, condition by condition;
* the **plausible range**: the high end assumes every unevidenced condition is
  met wherever the taxon's own data meet the criterion's gate (an area
  threshold, the D2 restriction, a small population).

The proposal is the **best estimate**, a decision of AOPK (D7) under §3.2.3,
which leaves the attitude to uncertainty to the institution running the
assessment. Uncertainty never moves the proposal. A proposal whose plausible
range holds both a non-threatened category (LC, NT) and a threatened one (VU,
EN, CR) is flagged **uncertain**. That is the case §10.1 describes: "If the
range of plausible categories include both LC and VU (or EN), the taxon can be
classified as NT, unless the best estimate is VU (or EN)". The flag says when NT
may be chosen. A range from LC to CR adds a **DD flag** (§10.1, §10.4). Choosing
NT or DD on uncertainty is the assessor's decision, "based on their level of
risk tolerance" (§10.4). ndopred proposes NT itself only where a criterion is
nearly met (§10.1 examples).

**Triage.** Every row gets a place in the expert queue from the highest
category its plausible range reaches: 1 where CR or EN is possible (or an RE
candidate), 2 where VU is possible (or a DD candidate), 3 for NT, 4 for an
**LC candidate**. A taxon is an LC candidate only when no criterion is met even
with every unknown subcriterion met. It is never LC without an expert: the
review (section 3) allows Rapid LC only as a low-priority preselection, since an
undetected decline is the risk a wide range does not exclude.

Values that are conventions rather than IUCN rules are set in
`ndopred_config()` and labelled there: the decline tolerance, the NT margins,
the RE-candidate period and the indicative D2 figures.

## 7. Criterion A

Thresholds are 90/70/50 % for A1 and 80/50/30 % for A2–A4, inclusive. The window
is 10 years or three generations, whichever is longer; past reductions (A2) are
not capped at 100 years, which §5.2 applies to projections only. The reduction
indication comes from the trend estimate (section 4): its tier, estimate and
interval, with basis (c) for occupancy and basis (b) for standardized counts or
NDOP counts. It is listed with what it still needs, because the number of
records changes with recording effort (§4.10.8). An assessor's reduction is
evidence and replaces the indication. A1 needs the causes to be reversible,
understood and ceased; otherwise the reduction is evaluated under A2.

## 8. Criterion B

The area threshold must be met (EOO < 100 / 5,000 / 20,000 km², AOO < 10 / 500 /
2,000 km²) **and at least two of** (a) severe fragmentation or ≤ 1 / 5 / 10
locations, (b) continuing decline, (c) extreme fluctuations. The conditions are
checked at every level whose area threshold is met, because (a) depends on the
level: a taxon with EOO 50 km² and four locations is EN, not "CR minus one
condition". Subindices under (b) come from what was measured or evidenced: (i)
from the change in alpha-hull EOO, (ii) from the trend estimate of AOO or
occupancy, (iii) only from the assessor, (iv) from the change in clusters, (v)
from counts. A decline in (i) or (ii) is indicated only when the whole interval
of the change lies below the decline tolerance (default 5 %), ruled out when it
lies above, and unknown otherwise.

**Locations** come from the evidence: the number of threat-defined locations
with its basis, either the most serious plausible threat over the whole range
or one of the §4.11 options for parts it does not affect. Option (a) means the
number of locations is not used, so the location subcriteria are not met; with
no plausible threat at all, "the subcriteria that refer to the number of
locations will not be met" (§4.11). The cluster count is only an indication: it
may support a proposal, and threat-defined locations are then listed as
needed.

## 9. Criteria C and D

C: fewer than 250 / 2,500 / 10,000 mature individuals, with either C1 (an
estimated continuing decline of 25 % in 3 years or 1 generation, 20 % in 5 years
or 2 generations, 10 % in 10 years or 3 generations, whichever is longer, up to
100 years) or C2 (a continuing decline in mature individuals and a(i) no
subpopulation over 50 / 250 / 1,000, a(ii) at least 90 / 95 / 100 % in one
subpopulation, or b extreme fluctuations). The observed rate is re-projected onto
each category's own period at a constant proportional rate (§4.5.1). C1 needs an
*estimated* decline, so it is met only from evidence or from a standardized
monitoring series (T3), never from opportunistic counts.

D: CR and EN **D** below 50 and 250 mature individuals; VU **D1** below 1,000.
**D2** (VU) needs the restriction (AOO typically < 20 km² or typically ≤ 5
locations) **and** a specified plausible threat able to make the taxon CR or EX
in a very short time (§8). "Simply meeting the suggested (or any other)
threshold for AOO or number of locations is not sufficient", and literal use
"results in massive over-listing" (§8). The threat must be described in words;
a bare yes is refused. A restricted taxon without one is a D2 candidate.

NDOP counts are minimum observed values and NDOP localities stand in for
subpopulations (§4.2, §4.3), so both are indications. `evaluate_pop` decides
whether NDOP counts may be used at all. The total is each locality's most recent
count, not a sum of maxima from different years; the latest census year and the
per-locality maxima are its range.

**Extreme fluctuations** (§4.7) need variation greater than one order of
magnitude **and** a recurring pattern of increases and decreases; "an observed
decline should not be considered as a fluctuation unless there is evidence for
this" (§4.6). Whether the change is in the population or in recording can only
be judged from a consistent-effort series, so `extreme_fluctuation` (a ratio ≥
10, at least two reversals, at least five years) is diagnosed only from
standardized monitoring counts (T3) and is unknown otherwise.

## 10. RE, DD and NE

* **RE.** A taxon with no current records and no record for longer than
  `re_candidate_years` is proposed as an **RE candidate**, with documented
  surveys listed as needed. Regional Guidelines v4.0 III.14 define RE as "no
  reasonable doubt that the last individual potentially capable of reproduction
  within the region has died or has disappeared", and leave any time limit to
  the regional authority; Guidelines §11.3 gives the probability models.
* **DD.** Proposed only as a candidate for a taxon with records but none in the
  current window and nothing else to go on, and flagged when the plausible
  range spans LC to CR (§10.1). DD requires the assessor to document all five
  criteria (§10.4).
* **NE.** A taxon with no usable records has not been evaluated (§10.4). A
  failed download gives no proposal at all, never DD or NE.

A taxon recorded in the comparison window but not in the current one is
proposed under A2c from the indicated loss, with current occurrence listed as
needing evidence (§11.2 prefers A2 for recent disappearances).

# Part III. From a proposal to an approved category

## 11. Expert evidence

Expert evidence is one table, kept apart from the NDOP data, with a row per
piece of evidence (`evidence_fields()` lists the fields; `evidence_template()`
writes a CSV or XLSX to fill offline; the single-taxon app writes the same
table). Every row carries its author, date and justification, and recommended
sources; numbers are `min`/`best`/`max` with a qualifier (observed, estimated,
projected, inferred, suspected; §3.1). The latest entry for a field is the one
in force, and `write_evidence()` stores each version as a new dated file, so an
assessment can be traced and rerun.

What the evidence holds, and how the engine reads it:

* **conditions and numbers** (severe fragmentation, continuing decline,
  fluctuations, mature individuals, subpopulations, a reduction with its
  basis and type): evidence, replacing the indications (section 5);
* **threats** (AOPK, D6: filled in by the experts), with **threat-defined
  locations** and their basis (section 8), and the **D2 threat** (section 9);
* **records** to exclude or re-include, by `ID_NALEZ`;
* the **generation length** of the taxon, and its current window where it
  differs;
* the **regional step**: origin and status, reproduction since, the global
  category and share, the answers to questions 3a–3f (section 12);
* criterion **E**, only from the assessor, with its sources;
* the **final category** and its **approvals** (section 13).

## 12. The regional step

A national Red List follows three steps (RG IV.1, Figure 1): decide which
regional populations to assess, apply the criteria to the regional population
(step two, the engine), and adjust the result for conspecific populations
outside the region.

**Step one** (`regional_eligibility()`, RG IV.2 and Annex 3). The criteria apply
"only to wild populations inside their natural range and to populations
resulting from benign introductions". Not Applicable (NA), and not assessed:

* introduced taxa;
* vagrants ("Vagrant taxa should NOT be assessed");
* occasional breeders that regularly become regionally extinct;
* colonizers until they have reproduced in the region "for several years
  (typically for at least 10 consecutive years)" (`colonizer_years`);
* taxa below an optional filter on the share of the global population
  (`regional_filter_share`, off until AOPK sets one).

As in the flowchart, an answer the assessor does not know leads to assessment.
Visitors are assessed, as visiting populations.

**Step three** (`regional_adjustment()`, RG IV.4, Figure 3, Table 1). Breeding
populations: if there is (3a) significant immigration of propagules likely to
reproduce, and it is not (3b) expected to decrease, the category is downlisted;
if it is expected to decrease (or that is unknown) and (3c) the regional
population is a sink, it is uplisted. Visiting populations are downlisted only
when conditions are deteriorating neither (3d) outside nor (3e) inside the
region and (3f) the breeding population can rescue them, which a taxon listed
globally under D cannot. "If it is unknown whether or not extra-regional
populations influence the extinction risk of the regional population, the
category from step two should be kept unaltered." A change is normally one
step, two for expanding populations at the edge of their range, more only in
extremely rare cases. EX, EW, RE, DD, NE and NA are never adjusted. An adjusted
category carries a degree sign, `VU°`, which "should be interpreted as being
equivalent to the same category" (RG V.3).

Every row reports the regional category, the reason from step one and the
step-three answers, and the global category with the share of the global
population in the region, `?` when unknown (RG V.4).

## 13. The final category and approval

**The final category** is the assessor's. `final_assessment()` checks it
against what the evidence and the measured data support on their own, without
the indications from the records, and with the same regional step applied. It
flags a threatened category above that, a criterion named but not met, a
category below a threatened one the evidence meets, DD where the evidence meets
a threatened category (§10.3), RE without documented surveys or before 1500 AD
(RG III.14; §11.3), EX or EW at national level, and NA without eligibility
evidence. A departure from the proposal is noted with its justification.

**Approval.** Group experts, conservationists and taxonomists trained in Red
List assessment, approve the final category (AOPK, D9), as approval rows in the
evidence file. Without an approval dated on or after the final category, it is
reported as *awaiting approval*, not as final. An approved category the checks
do not support is reported as "approved; inconsistent with the evidence", so
the inconsistency stays visible.

`species_card()` puts one assessment on one HTML page: proposal and range,
final category with approvals and checks, parameters with bounds, every
criterion with the rule applied and what decided it, the evidence with its
authors, the record IDs used and excluded, open questions and the versions.

# Part IV. Checking the method

## 14. Benchmark against ConR, redlistr and red

`compare_tools()` runs the current-window records of a taxon through ndopred
and through ConR 2.1, redlistr 2.1.0 and red 1.6.3, the tools the review
compares (section 3); `inst/benchmark/benchmark_tools.R` runs it on the pilot
taxa. On three taxa (NDOP exports of September and October 2026, current window
2010–2026):

| Taxon | Points | EOO km² (ndopred / ConR / redlistr / red) | AOO km² (ndopred / ConR / redlistr / red) | Clusters / ConR locations | B: ndopred best / plausible max / ConR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Onthophagus medius* | 21 | 6,552 / 6,530 / 6,552 / 6,551 | 28 / 32 / 28 / 36 | 6 / 6 | LC or NT / EN / VU |
| *Protaetia cuprea* | 1,325 | 85,470 / 85,191 / 85,470 / 85,474 | 3,120 / 3,268 / 3,168 / 3,144 | 346 / 437 | LC or NT / LC or NT / LC or NT |
| *Bombina bombina* | 17,163 | 74,699 / 74,455 / 74,699 / 74,703 | 8,036 / 8,892 / 8,220 / 8,204 | 225 / 559 | LC or NT / LC or NT / LC or NT |

* **EOO** agrees exactly with redlistr and within 0.01 % with red; ConR is
  0.3 % smaller, from its cylindrical equal-area projection.
* **AOO** is lowest in ndopred, as a minimum over origins should be: redlistr
  jitters the grid only for 150 cells or fewer, red uses one grid. ConR is 5 to
  14 % higher: its 2 km cells are square in the cylindrical projection, not on
  the ground, at 50° N. The benchmark also found that the 4 × 4 origin search
  could miss the minimum by a cell, which led to the exact search (section 2).
* **Category B** differs by design. ConR assumes a continuing decline when none
  is given and counts locations on a 10 km grid; ndopred assumes nothing. For
  *O. medius* the best estimate is therefore LC or NT under B. The plausible
  maximum, EN, takes the unknown (a) and (b) as met; ConR takes (b) as met but
  counts 6 grid locations, too many for EN (at most 5), and so gives VU.

The tests cross-check EOO against redlistr (exactly) and ConR (within 1 %), AOO
against redlistr's jittered grids, and the category against ConR where both
rules agree.

## 15. Pilot validation

The review (section 9) asks for a pilot on two insect groups, one well recorded
(e.g. butterflies) and one poorly recorded (e.g. saproxylic beetles), against
**blinded** expert assessments, with false "threatened" and false
"non-threatened" proposals counted separately: one accuracy over all taxa
hides which error is made. `inst/validation/pilot_validation.R` runs it from an
expert table (taxon, category, group, assessor, blinded):

* `validate_against_experts()` compares the proposals (after the regional step)
  with the expert categories: exact agreement, the same threat status, false
  threatened, false non-threatened, sensitivity and specificity, how often the
  plausible range covers the expert category, and a confusion matrix, overall
  and per group.
* `filter_stability()` reassesses each taxon without unvalidated records
  (`VEROH` 0), without less credible ones (3), without literature and
  collection records, without positions less precise than 2 km, with 10 % of
  the records dropped at random, and, with `region_variants()`, without one
  region at a time; it reports where the category or the threat status
  changes.

The expert assessments are not in hand yet, so the comparison has not been
run. The stability test alone already shows what it is for. On the three
benchmark taxa, dropping literature and collection records, imprecise
positions or 10 % of the records changes no proposal, but unvalidated records
matter: all 25 records of *Onthophagus medius* were unvalidated (`VEROH` 0) at
download, so without them it cannot be evaluated (NE); 1,281 of the 1,402
usable records of *Protaetia cuprea* were, and without them the proposal moves
from LC to NT with a range of LC-EN. *Bombina bombina* is stable under every
filter.

## 16. The export

`batch_assess()` and the bulk app write one row per taxon. The Czech column
names AOPK already uses are unchanged; new columns follow them. Every column is
described in `export_dictionary()`, with its layer (section "Four states") and
a candidate field of an IUCN SIS export, to be checked against the current SIS
schema before any transfer.

```{r dictionary}
d <- export_dictionary()
knitr::kable(d[, c("batch_column", "app_column", "layer", "description")],
             col.names = c("batch_assess()", "Bulk app", "Layer", "Meaning"))
```

## 17. Known limitations

* NDOP is an opportunistic database. AOO, EOO and cluster counts depend on
  recording effort (§4.10.8), and counts are minimum observed values (§4.3).
* Without an effort layer a trend is T0: a raw change, effort-blind. T1 still
  carries target-species bias (review §7.1); for large groups the effort layer
  is a random sample of cadastral units. T2 assumes a linear trend in occupancy
  and reports convergence (Rhat). The overlap of the AOPK windows damps every
  change. Negative findings count as zero counts in T3 series; T1 and T2 do not
  use them yet.
* Generation lengths are a 1-year placeholder for every group until AOPK
  refines the table.
* NDOP data come only through rndop (AOPK, D4), which exports no visit
  identifier and no source type: visits are rebuilt from date, locality and an
  anonymous observer code, list length is the detection covariate of T2, and
  literature records are recognised heuristically.
* Threats, and so threat-defined locations and the D2 threat, come only from
  the assessor (AOPK, D6). Criterion E is taken only from the assessor.
* One assessment covers a taxon's NDOP records as one regional population.
  Breeding and visiting populations that RG IV.2 would assess separately are
  not separated: NDOP records carry no breeding/visiting distinction, and
  evidence is keyed by taxon name.
* The pilot validation against blinded expert assessments is built but not yet
  run.
